name: Job
bio:
Job was a blameless and upright man from the land of Uz who feared God and shunned evil. He had seven sons, three daughters, and vast wealth in livestock, making him the greatest man in the East; he regularly offered sacrifices on his children's behalf out of concern they might have sinned.

## 📖 Core Story: The Testing of Job

When Satan appeared before the LORD and accused Job of serving God only for the blessings he received, the LORD permitted Satan to take everything from him, short of touching Job himself, to prove his integrity. In a single day, Job lost his oxen and donkeys to Sabean raiders, his sheep to fire from the sky, his camels to Chaldean raiders, and all ten of his children when a windstorm collapsed the house where they were feasting. Job tore his robe, shaved his head, and fell to the ground in mourning, yet worshipped God, declaring, "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; may the name of the LORD be praised." Through all this, Job did not sin or blame God (Job 1:1-22). His further testing, his debates with his friends, and his eventual restoration are told in detail in the chapters ahead.

 Satan then returned before the LORD, claiming Job's integrity would collapse if his own body were afflicted; granted permission to touch Job but not kill him, Satan covered him with painful sores from head to foot. Job's wife urged him to curse God and die, but he refused, insisting they must accept hardship from God as readily as blessing, and still did not sin. Hearing of his suffering, three friends — Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite — came to mourn with him; finding him barely recognizable, they wept, tore their robes, and sat with him in silence for seven days and nights, so great was his grief (Job 2:1-13).

 Breaking his silence, Job cursed the day he was born, wishing he had never lived to see such suffering. Over three cycles of debate, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar each insisted his suffering must be deserved punishment for hidden sin, and Job answered each in turn — maintaining his innocence, accusing his friends of being miserable comforters who wounded him with words instead of helping, demanding to bring his case directly before God, and wrestling aloud with why the wicked often prosper while the righteous suffer. He closed with a long, final defense recalling his former honor and compassion toward the poor and vulnerable, and swearing a detailed oath of innocence covering lust, dishonesty, idolatry, and mistreatment of others, daring God to answer him if he had sinned as his friends claimed (Job 3-31).

 The LORD then answered Job out of a whirlwind, overwhelming him with a sweeping tour of creation's wonders — from the foundations of the earth to the behavior of wild animals and the untamable sea monsters Behemoth and Leviathan — to show how far Job's understanding fell short of God's own. Job, humbled, admitted he had spoken of things beyond his knowledge and repented in dust and ashes, having now encountered God rather than merely heard of him. The LORD then rebuked Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar for misrepresenting him, and had them offer sacrifices while Job prayed for them; once Job prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his fortunes twofold, giving him twice his former livestock and seven new sons and three daughters — Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren-happuch, famed as the most beautiful women in the land, to whom Job gave an inheritance alongside their brothers. Job lived another 140 years, saw four generations of descendants, and died old and full of days (Job 38:1-42:17).
